AMAR

ZOHAR
PLASTIQUES INC.

Plaintiff

v.

IMAFLEX INC.

Defendant

_____________________________________________________________________

JUDGMENT

______________________________________________________________________

INTRODUCTION

1
.         The Plaintiff
Imaflex extrudes and
distributes blow film, which is sheet plastic, opaque or transparent, that it
sells to bag manufacturers.  Defendant Zohar is in the same business.  The
individual Defendants were Zohar's principals at the time of the events that
gave rise to the present litigation.

2
.         Imaflex's
founders and its shareholders, directors and officers at the same time were
Giuseppe (Joe) Abbandonato, Gerald (Gerry) Phelps, and Tony Abbandonato, all of
whom had long experience in the plastic film industry.

3
.         Imaflex was a
start-up business.  It possessed some used equipment it had reconditioned and
know how, but it was short on capital.  Its principals therefore believed they
could begin operations more rapidly by sharing facilities with, Zohar, an
established business which then had surplus manufacturing capacity.

4
.         On December 9
1991,
Imaflex and Zohar, entered an
agreement, Exhibit P-2, (the "Agreement") for a term of three years
whereby Imaflex's extrusion equipment (the "Oerlikon line") would be
brought to Zohar's
premises situated at the corner of 4035 St. Ambroise and 137 St.
Ferdinand in the City of Montreal (the "Premises") and there
dedicated to Zohar's production requirements,
while some of Zohar's equipment located there (the "Dolci line")
would be dedicated to Imaflex's production requirements.

5
.         Use
of the Dolci line was made available to Imaflex
for production from about mid-April 1992, and full commercial production on it
began in July of that year, while
the Oerlikon line was made available to Zohar for
production in January 1992.

6
.         The commercial relationship of the
parties was not a happy one.  By autumn 1992 Joe Abbandonato was complaining
bitterly about the inadequacy of the workers Zohar had provided to work the
Dolci line for Imaflex.  In December 1992 the parties agreed to a parting of
the ways on terms to be negotiated.

7
.         It was not until June 1993, however,
that Imaflex having been pressed for months to commit to a departure date
indicated to Zohar that it would probably move out by September 1, 1993.

8
.         When that date came, with Imaflex
still on the Premises and owing Zohar more than $30,000, which it was
threatening not to pay for various reasons, Zohar ceased all further production
and locked Imaflex out.

9
.         The present litigation ensued.
Imaflex has made the following claims of which a detailed calculation is set
forth in its summary of final claims :

10
.       Zohar for its part counter-sued
for damages in the amount of $637,204.  In a separate action it has also
claimed on account fees of $36,000 owed to it by Imaflex for producing the
latter's film on the Dolci line.  The two actions were joined and the present
judgment disposes of both.

11
.       Trial of the case lasted 16 days and
counsel thereafter filed written arguments.  The proof was highly detailed,
technical and quantitative. Rather than set out the factual circumstances of
each claim and the detailed reasons the parties advanced to justify them in the
main body of the present judgment, which would make for very tedious reading,
the Court has annexed them in the form of the lengthy written arguments of
counsel which it has edited only lightly.

SECTION 1 - DOWN TIME DUE TO
LATE START-UP

Disposition of claim

12
.       The claim is rejected.  It is the
former
Civil Code
that governs the parties' relationship.  By virtue of Article
1067 C.C.L.C. a written notice of default was necessary to render the
Defendants liable in damages for delay in putting the Dolci line into
operation.  In the circumstances, its absence and almost two years of inaction
is presumptive that Imaflex did not consider that Zohar's conduct, consistent
with its interpretation of the Agreement, which was silent on the matter, gave
rise to any actionable breach of contract.

13
.

Imaflex now says that it did
not want to create ill will by insisting on what it claims were its contractual
rights at the beginning of a new relationship but chose to do so only at the
onset of litigation a couple of years later.  Assuming it truly viewed the
Agreement as it now claims it did, then regardless of its motives, it must live
with the result of its passivity during the only time it could have done
something to cause the situation to be rectified.

SECTION 2 - QUALITY CLAIMS

Disposition of claim

14
.       The entire claim of
$2,153.64
is
granted.  The proof Imaflex brought came from independent and credible
sources.  While the language of paragraph 10 of the Agreement indicates that
the defective product must be the result of formulas or control checks not
being followed, or proper machine settings not being made, the nature of the
defects themselves and the sources of the complaint are such as to create the
presumption that those were indeed their causes without requiring Imaflex to
prove positively that such was the case.

15
.       The burden of proof then shifts to
Zohar to establish that the defects were attributable to some cause other than
its own fault, such as the instructions or training given by Imaflex being
incorrect or its raw materials inadequate.  It did not discharge that burden.

SECTION 3 - SHIPPING

Disposition of claim

16
.       The claim is rejected in its entirety.

17
.       There is nothing in the evidence
beyond Imalex's after the fact assertions to show that Zohar was aware of its
particular shipping requirements or the special needs of its clientele.  If any
particular scheduling requirements were necessary, Imaflex has only itself to
blame for not stipulating them in the Agreement.

18
.       Its assertion that for purposes of the
Agreement Zohar was a transporter and therefore bound by the provisions of a
contract of carriage is not sustainable.  Zohar is clearly not a professional
transporter nor did it even implicitly hold itself out as such.

19
.       The parties agreed that Zohar would
provide local shipping without saying more. It is therefore their behaviour
that gives substance to their agreement in the absence of language itself
providing a guide.

20
.       What was involved here was a sharing
of facilities.  Zohar was receiving Imaflex as a paying guest in its own
establishment, already a going concern with its own dynamics and patterns, not
as its partner.

21
.       If anything, the default
interpretation should be that Imaflex would have had to accommodate itself to
those existing circumstances rather than that Zohar should go to unusual or
special lengths to accommodate Imaflex.

22
.       The parties' obligations must not be
seen as going beyond what the Agreement and their own behaviour would
indicate.  Certainly, there is nothing in the proof to establish that equity,
law or usage would create the kinds of rights in favour of Imaflex it now
asserts.

23
.       Its invocation of Article 1024
C.C.L.Q. is in the circumstances a residual argument conceived after the fact
because there is nothing concrete in the evidence to support its claim for
extra shipping costs.

24
.       Its representatives' assertions that
they complained about the situation verbally and that they did not want to
offend their more powerful host by making specific written demands at the
relevant time that were consistent with what they now claim to be their rights
are unpersuasive.

Local shipping

25
.       The claim is unfounded.  Zohar's
obligation must be seen as going no farther than to combine Imaflex's shipments
with its own truck deliveries on Mondays and to add a second truck for Imaflex
on Wednesdays.  If Imaflex had special requirements for speedier deliveries, it
was only fair that it should make its own arrangements and absorb the extra
costs incurred.  That is in fact what it did.  It cannot now come back and
claim the same costs as its contractual right.  The Agreement provides for no
such thing, and in the circumstances lends itself to no such
interpretation.

26
.       Moreover, Imaflex brought no proof
that the charges it now wants to recover were anything other than costs of
shipments made on days other than Monday or Wednesday.  The charges on the
latter days, one assumes, would normally have been made to Zohar rather than to
Imaflex, or the shipments would otherwise have been made in Zohar's own truck
and therefore not been charged.

Charges for scrap delivery and pick-ups

27
.       Again, this is a claim made after the
fact.  Imaflex now seeks recovery of amounts it paid to Zohar without any
protest that the proof reveals.  Because the Agreement is silent, one would
think that Imaflex would have protested from the start if the charges were
unacceptable to it either because they came within the scope of "local
shipping", or if they did not and had to be paid for on a
quantum
meruit
basis, because they were unreasonable.

28
.       In the latter connection, it contends
that some of the charges were excessive because Zohar's truck had a capacity to
carry its own scrap and Imaflex's in one load so that the extra trip to take
Imaflex's scrap to the recycler was unnecessary and deliberately planned so
that Zohar would pick up the extra $50 or so it would charge for it.  There is
no proof of that charge other than Joe Abbandonato's flat assertion offered
years later in the context of a bitter litigation that has left no stone
unturned.

29
.

The Court prefers to rely on
what the parties in fact did while they were performing the Agreement
routinely, rather than on their hindsight in adversarial circumstances as to
how it might have been performed more fairly.

Shipment of winder after September 2, 1993
shutdown

Transportation of resin from
second seizure

30
.       The Court is persuaded by Zohar's
argument that these are charges Imaflex would have had to incur anyway in the
normal course.

31
.       After all, it had been saying it
wanted to leave since September 1992, and Zohar was anxious for that to occur.
It would have been required to do so by December 9, 1993 in any case.

32
.       As for the winder, all the Court knows
is that it needed a repair and that it was shipped to Future Design Inc., a
specialist in Ontario, for that purpose.  Nothing in the proof persuades the
Court that it would have been possible for the winder to have been repaired
more conveniently and economically on the Premises before Imaflex moved out.
Would it have been cheaper for the technicians to travel to Montreal from
Ontario to do the work?

33
.       The winder was returned to Imaflex at
its new plant six weeks later at a cost of $200, not $400 as claimed, (the bill
of lading simply says "machinerie" with a handwritten note that half
the shipping charge of $400 relates to the "winder from Future").
These charges might well have been inevitable in any case.

34
.       There is nothing in the proof to
persuade the Court that there would not have been some resin to transport to a
new place of business.  (The fact that it was from a place other than the
Premises does not make a difference to the cost of transport since the place
was within a few blocks of the Premises.)  If it is true that Imaflex could, as
it asserts, have planned production so as to gradually use up the stored resin,
the Court has no idea of the rate at which this would likely have been done.
That would have depended on its order volume over the next three months, which
was not established.  The Court also presumes that it would have an immediate
need for resin on hand at its new Premises.

35
.       In sum, Imaflex has not discharged its
burden of proof with regard to its claim for shipping charges.

SECTION 4 - CONSULTING FEES

Disposition of claim

36
.

Imaflex's claim for
consulting fees is manifestly not sustainable for all the reasons set forth in
Zohar's arguments.  All the Agreement seems to indicate is that the services
would be provided as needed and at what ever cost the parties agreed to from
time to time.  Nothing obliged Zohar to take these services if it did not need
or want them.  It is significant that when Zohar indicated it would no longer
use the services, Imaflex did not protest.

SECTION 5 - ED O’HANLON PAY

Disposition of claim

37
.       The Defense did not contest this claim of
$414
,
and it is granted.

SECTION 6 - MISSING RESIN

Disposition of claim

38
.       The Court confesses that it experienced
considerable frustration in negotiating its way through the parties'
representations, most of which it found more distracting than helpful.  It
believes considerable time and money might have been saved if they and their
professional advisers had, rather than engage in polemics, in good faith and
with objectivity, simply tried together to reconcile diverging figures in what
at bottom is an exercise in calculation.

39
.       The Court concludes that the most objective and
reliable approach is that of Harel Drouin.  That is because it works from a
more recent data baseline that the parties themselves appear to have trusted.
Specifically, the Court observes that the monthly inventory sheets complied by
Imaflex itself, and with which Messrs. Tony Abbandonato and Gerry Phelps say
they were comfortable, form the basis of the report.

40
.       The starting point should therefore be the raw
material inventory on Imaflex's books as of June 30, 1993, not that of a year
earlier, especially since the parties subsequently made their correction to
inventory as of September 30, 1992.  From the latter date forward Imaflex's
representatives say they controlled the inventory to their satisfaction.

41
.       Joe Abbandonato tried to persuade the Court that
Imaflex was awaiting the termination of the Agreement before doing a final
reconciliation and that until then the methods of determining inventory were
somewhat improvised (throwing rocks at and knocking containers).  However, if
perfection was not the result, it is now too late for Imaflex to impugn its own
control methodology after the fact and make Zohar suffer for it.

42
.       The Court disagrees with Imaflex's counsel that
the raw materials inventory as of June 30, 1993 should be that suggested by
note 4 to Imaflex's finacial statements as of that date.  The statements,
prepared by Christian Dorais, were unaudited.

43
.       The Harel Drouin report, on the other hand, is
evidently based on Imaflex's own month-end inventory report as of that date.
(Annex 8 to the report).  The beginning inventory for purposes of calculating
the resin shortfall is, as stated in the report, therefore 117,977 pounds (page
10).  The Court agrees with Imaflex's counsel that all the other figures in the
calculation should remain, with the exception of the weekly start-up loss of
500 pounds which the Court calculated for nine weeks rather than eight, since
there are 62 days in July and August.

44
.       As a result, the theoretical raw materials
inventory as of September 2, 1993 should have been 161,812 pounds, not 162,312,
as stated in the report.  The reason the Court believes the report is reliable
in other respects is that it was prepared directly from the invoices for
production from Zohar to Imaflex for the period July 1, 1993 to September 2,
1993.

45
.       The raw materials purchased during the same
period were taken from suppliers' invoices, as were the quantities of recycled
materials.  Loss due to recycling was calculated directly from the recycler's
invoices.  The weekly loss due to start-up was calculated the same way as in
the Christian Dorais report.

46
.       From the theoretical inventory of 161,812 pounds,
the 133,915 pounds of inventory recovered from the seizure, as weighed and
counted by Imaflex's controller Jean Pierre Groulx on October 20 and 21, 1993,
is subtracted to leave a balance of missing raw materials of 27,897 pounds.

47
.       At the average blend rate of $0.4398 per pound
claimed by Imaflex, the loss to be covered is $12,269.

48
.       In the opinion of the Court, no credit should be
given to Zohar for the 13,630 pounds of seized clear repro that Imaflex was
forced to give up to it in order to avoid the time and cost of a contested
seizure.  Imaflex, without premises and faced with a serious business
interruption, had no practical choice but to do so.

49
.       It did not, however, renounce its claim on the
merits.  It simply granted mainlevée of a seizure without prejudice.  The issue
of properly determining missing inventory has remained outstanding from the
start of the present litigation nonetheless.

50
.       Imaflex's claim for the $5,372.50 paid for the
Christian Dorais report is denied.  The report was not especially helpful.
Furthermore, proper inventory controls and vigilance by Imaflex might have
enabled it to do without such a report.  The Court disagrees that in this
respect it was entirely at Zohar's mercy.  It could have itself imposed some
form of control on access to its silo resin, the two silos being entirely its
own for the duration of the Agreement.  As for inventory on the floor, it seems
that Imaflex could have established a uniform labeling system for its boxes and
run some kind of control list at more frequent intervals than monthly.  The
Court notes that it was quality issues that preoccupied Imaflex, not inventory
control.  After the correction as of September 30, 1992 it made no complaints
about missing inventory or lax control measures of Zohar.

51
.       The only really pertinent element contained in
the Christian Dorais report as far as the Court is concerned is the physical
inventory count done in October 1993, and that was the work of Imaflex's
employee, not Christian Dorais.

52
.       Imaflex's claim for the 25,650 pounds of finished
goods still under seizure calculated at the average 75 cent per pound selling
price to its customers is also rejected.  Imaflex asks to be declared the owner
of these goods.  It cannot do so and at the same time demand their selling
price.

53
.       For the foregoing reasons the Court awards
Imaflex the sum of
$12,269
for missing inventory.

SECTION 7 - REMOVAL OF RESIN FROM SILOS

Disposition of claim

54
.       Imaflex's claim is credible and appropriately
proven.  Since, moreover, it does not appear to be contested by Zohar, the
Court awards Imaflex
$2,032
.  Because these damages result directly from
the September 2, 1993 shutdown, itself due to the common fault of all the
Defendants, they are soldarily liable for this claim.

SECTION 8 - DOWN TIME DUE TO SEPTEMBER 2, 1993
SHUTDOWN

Disposition of claim

55
.       Zohar's reaction to the non-payment of its
invoices was excessive and abusive.

56
.       Imaflex had never promised to move out by
September 1, 1993 and certainly not under such rushed circumstances.
Considering the various facets of the Agreement, which contemplated an ongoing
functional relationship involving co-ordination of equipment, materials and
labour and a unique accounting arrangement, any departure, even premature, had
to be orderly.  Undoubtedly, that is why the parties would have contemplated a
mutual release in the event of the premature termination materializing as
expected.

57
.       In July 1993 Joe Abbandonato merely announced an
expected departure date, not a promised one, and made it clear that the actual
date would be commmunicated by formal notice.

58
.       It is also evident that Imaflex was trying in
good faith to find suitable alternate space, judging by the number of offers to
lease it made during summer 1993 that were entered in evidence.  The intent was
not to be confused with the act, however.  Until Imaflex was actually in a
position to move, it was entitled to stay on and benefit from Zohar's
facilities as provided for in the Agreement until its expiry in the normal
course, regardless of its expectation that it would leave earlier.  An
expectation is not to be confused with a promise.

59
.       The fact that Imaflex owed Zohar money did not
justify so extreme a reaction by the latter.  Imaflex may have been in default
to pay Zohar's bills but not egregiously so.  It had just paid more than
$5,000, leaving a balance of $31,319 of which only $9,224 was in the 31-60 day
aged receipt category.  The balance was in the 30-day category, the term
provided for in the Agreement for the payment of Zohar's accounts.

60
.       In spite of a stormy relationship, Imaflex had in
the main met its monetary responsibilities.  Yet, Zohar in effect took the law
into its own hands and precipitously terminated the relationship.  There is no
other way to characterize its reaction.  It did not merely suspend production
after a warning, but evicted Imaflex without first putting it in default to
cure the breach it says justified its actions.  By those actions it repudiated
the contract, confirmed by its resistance of Imaflex's efforts to reinstate it.

61
.       The exception of
non adimpleti contractus

must be applied by a debtor of obligations in a manner that is proportionate to
the non-performance of the corresponding obligations of its creditor.  This is
nothing more than a particular application of a principle of good faith
required in the performance of contractual obligations which found expression
in the reference to equity contained in Article 1024 C.C.L.C.  The
Civil
Code of Quebec
now expressly recognizes the requirement of proportionality
in
Article 1591
:

1591.

Where the obligations arising from a synallagmatic contract are
exigible and one of the parties fails to perform his obligation to a
substantial degree or does not offer to perform it, the other party may refuse
to perform his correlative obligation to a corresponding degree, unless he is
bound by law, the will of the parties or usage
to
perform first.

62
.       Preventing access to a co-venturer's property and
records, then removing much of the property clandestinely is no way to tell it
that if it mends its ways, all will be forgiven and it will be welcome back.

63
.       Imaflex is therefore entitled to appropriate
damages arising from Zohar's premature and abusive termination of the
Agreement, in itself a breach of contract.
[1]

64
.       The Court considers that Imaflex's claim of $700
a day for lost gross profit during the 89 day period between September 2, 1993
and December 1, 1993 is reasonable in extent and calculation, considering that
it took until the latter date before it could resume production at new
premises.

65
.       The daily amount is very conservative when
compared with its calculation of gross daily profits for the same three months
in 1992.

66
.       It is also consistent with Gerry Phelps's
calculation of daily pounds produced which was based on historic data.  Both of
these estimates hold up, independently of the distracting quagmire of
calculations to which Imaflex's attempt to claim missing inventory has given
rise.

67
.       The Court therefore awards
$62,300
to
Imaflex, which all Defendants are to pay solidarily.  Even though the personal
Defendants were acting as the representatives of Zohar, by common accord, they
intentionally caused Zohar to deprive Imaflex of access to and the free
disposition of its property.  By their conduct they also created a reasonable
apprehension that Zohar intended to appropriate Imaflex's property for itself
without legal process.

68
.       They were not the servants of Zohar in this
regard but its masters.  It must also be remembered that because Zohar was
owned by themselves or their families they had a personal expectation of gain
from acting as they did.  They therefore share the fault in common with Zohar
and by virtue of Article 1106 C.C.L.Q.
[2]

they are solidarily liable for the damages Imaflex suffered.

69
.       Under the
Civil Code of Lower Canada
,
which governs the rights and obligations of the parties in the present case,

it was possible to combine contractual responsibility with delictual
responsibility.  The liability is therefore common to all the Defendants, being
extra-contractual for the individuals and either contractual or
extra-contractual for Zohar.

SECTION 9 - EXTRAORDINARY COMMUNICATION CHARGES

Disposition of claim

70
.       The Court believes Zohar's argument is correct.
In comparing Messrs. Gerry Phelps's and Joe Abbandonato's phone bills before
and after the shutdown, Imaflex has used the wrong point of comparison.  Its
own communication costs would have been the appropriate reference. The claim is
therefore rejected.

SECTION 10 - REPAIRS BY IMAFLEX OF OERLIKON

Disposition of the claim

71
.       Confronted with contradictory proof as
to who is responsible for the post-termination repairs and why, the Court is
left with only the presumption expressed in Article 1623 C.C.L.C.:

1623.   The lessee must return the thing
in the condition in which he received it, with the exception of changes
resulting from normal aging, fortuitous event or irresistible force.

The
condition of the thing may be established by a description made by the parties.

When there is no such description,
the lessee is presumed to have received it in good condition, saving proof to
the contrary
.
(underlining added)

72
.       The proof is uncontradicted that the
Oerlikon line was in good condition when received by Zohar, having been
disassembled and completely rebuilt, then test run before being put into
commercial operation.  In any case, the legal presumption is to that effect and
Zohar has not rebutted it, nor has it offered any proof that the repairs were
necessitated by normal aging.  A mere assertion to that effect in argument is
not proof.

73
.       The above obligation to return in good
condition is one of result.  In this connection, the quality of the maintenance
program is therefore irrelevant.  What counts is the state of the equipment
when the contract ends.

74
.       Zohar must therefore pay for the
repair of the Oerlikon and related equipment.  Even if it could have done some
of the repairs itself (notably the cleaning), it had a reasonable opportunity
to do so but did not.

75
.       Imaflex cannot, however, recover all
that it claims under this head.  To start with, the repair of the Queen's
winder for $4,011 had not been made as of February 18, 1994 when the equipment
had already been in production since December 1, 1993 at Imaflex's new
premises.  Imaflex cannot recover an expense it did not incur.

76
.       Moreover, the cost of replacing the
barrel and feed screw in the amount of $15,389 is excessive and would represent
an improvement paid for by Zohar.  Based on the testimony of Robert Krycki, the
vendor of the Oerlikon to Imaflex, the two parts could have been rebuilt at a
total cost of $5,000-$6,000.

77
.       The Court will therefore award only
$5,500 for these items, inclusive of the cost of rebuilding the feed screw for
$1,220 that had been incurred before Imaflex decided to replace the parts.

78
.       The total claim awarded to Imaflex for
post–termination repairs is therefore
$9,208.33
. (Exhibit P-100,
$24,328.33 – [$4,011 + $1,220 + $15,389] + $5,500).  No G.S.T. will be allowed,
since Imaflex could claim the G.S.T. it paid on the repairs as input tax
credits on its remittances of the G.S.T. it collected.  Imaflex is not a
supplier of goods or services to Zohar in this connection but a creditor of
damages.

SECTION 11 - USE OF OERLIKON BY ZOHAR AFTER
SEPTEMBER 2, 1993

Disposition of the claim

79
.       Zohar admits that 42,000 pounds of
film were produced on the Oerlikon line between September 2 and September 14.
Serge Afflalo's explanation of how this came to be was consistent and
credible.

80
.       He told the Court that the equipment
was used on September 6, 7, 8, 13 and 14 and for a small order on September 10,
in each case to produce black sheet film for conversion into garbage bags.

81
.       This was due to the fact, he relates,
that the machine was already set up to process black resin, and Zohar did not
want to contaminate any of its five other extrusion lines, then being used for
clear plastic.  This would have engendered considerable down time for cleaning
afterwards.  Imaflex had not yet come to pick up its machine, so he decided to
take advantage of its continuing availability.

82
.       Clearly, he was consulting production
records to make his assertions.  If Zohar's previous lawyers stated in
correspondence that production records were unavailable in fulfilling undertakings
arising from the examination of Jules Amar, the misrepresentation is not
imputable to Mr. Afflalo personally.

83
.       Furthermore, just because Mr. Afflalo
affirmed the Oerlikon line was used 24 hours a day before the shutdown, it does
not follow that such was the case afterwards.  The Court finds his testimony
credible in this regard, neither self-serving nor evasive.

84
.       The most that any of Imaflex's
witnesses could observe was use during three days only, while Mr. Afflalo
admits to five and a half, when he might have done as much only for three.

85
.       It must be remembered that Imaflex has
also claimed (and is awarded) $700 a day for the 89 days of down time it
suffered as a result of the shutdown.  Claiming additional indemnification on
any basis other than Zohar's actual production using the machine would be a
form of double counting, and clearly unfair.

86
.       Given the termination of the Agreement
by Zohar's own actions, it would be patently unfair not to compensate Imaflex
for the additional and unauthorized use made of its equipment.

87
.       The tolling approach, i.e. charging at
a rate per pound recognized by Imaflex's witnesses Gerry Phelps and Ken
Ahmedkhan appears sound.  Gerry Phelps's testimony and Exhibit P-123 showing
that Imaflex itself charged its customers, not an hourly rate, but rather a fee
of 25 cents a pound, including labour, is useful here.

88
.       The contract rate of 17 cents a pound
is inappropriate, since that reduced rate reflected to some extent the
availability of the Oerlikon line to Zohar, as well as other services provide
to it by Imaflex.

89
.       The labour charge calculated by Mr.
Phelps as four cents a pound must be deducted to make a net fee of 21 cents a
pound.

90
.       Multiplied by 42,000 pounds the total
amount due to Imaflex for unauthorized use of its equipment is
$8,820.

SECTION 12 - ELECTRICAL INSTALLATION

Disposition of the claim

91
.       The Court prefers the proof that Imaflex offers.
Exhibit P-4 is categorical: the parties agreed the sum of $5,004.48 would be
reimbursed when Imaflex moved.  The safety concern arising from removing the
main breakers, and Mr. Afflalo's inconsistency as to whether both breakers or
one only were removed, cause the Court to place its faith in the parties'
agreement at the outset.  Imaflex's affirmation that neither breaker was
removed is to be retained.

92
.       The Court therefore admits its claim for
$5,004.48
.

SECTION 13 - LOSS OF REPUTATION AND GOODWILL

Disposition of claim

93
.       The Court agrees with Zohar's
arguments in their entirety.  Imaflex's claims in this respect were
over-reaching, speculative and wasteful of time and money.  Its witnesses did
not strike the Court as possessing the necessary objectivity.  None of the
customers whose patronage was lost had any fixed term contractual relationship.
They could have left for any number of reasons.  Eight years after the fact,
the Court is loath to believe that it was for any reason imputable exclusively
to Zohar.  The same holds true of the bankers' testimony.  It struck the Court
as almost rehearsed.

94
.       Now that Imaflex is successful, it is
a stretch to conclude at this point that it experienced financing difficulties
or had to pay more interest solely because of its difficulties with Zohar.
Perhaps Imaflex itself improved its management, or the market itself may have
improved.

95
.       The manufacture and distribution of
plastic film, a packaging product, appears to the Court to be a highly
competitive and volatile industry, where customer loyalty may be fleeting.

96
.       Furthermore, Roger Michel of the
Business Development Bank was perhaps correct in his understanding of the
perspective of the present litigation expressed by that bank's outside
counsel.  The bank's lawyer predicted that the litigation would last for years
and in the end no one would win.

97
.       That appears to have been an accurate
prediction if one considers the financial result relative to the time and
effort consumed, needlessly in the Court's view, on complicated financial and
technical issues that it was necessary to exhaustively analyse after the
fact.

98
.       Imaflex's claim for damage to loss of reputation,
inclusive of the legal fees it claims for the legal opinion to its bank, is
rejected.

SECTION 14 - EXEMPLARY DAMAGES

Disposition of the claim

99
.       Even allowing that Zohar's foremost
intention was to protect its interests rather than to harm Imaflex, its
behaviour was abusive and must be sanctioned by the Court through punitive
damages.

100
.     It is not malice as such that merits
the punishment but the fact that Zohar acted, with such reckless disregard for
the rights of its co-venturer.

101
.     Zohar might perhaps have advanced a
legitimate argument that it did not have to continue production as long as
Imaflex remained in arrears as the Agreement approached termination,
particularly when the non-payment was accompanied with the rather bellicose
threats of Joe Abbandonato.

102
.     What it cannot justify, however, even
in those circumstances, is the exclusion of Imaflex and any of its principals
from the Premises, the retention of finished goods needed by Imaflex to honour
orders to its customers when there is no such right of retention in law and the
goods retained were disproportionate in value to the arrears past the
contractual term of 30 days, and finally, the removal of Imaflex's raw
materials from the Premises without the latter's knowledge or consent, and with
no attempt made to segregate them from its own.

103
.     These acts constituted an intentional
infringement of Imaflex's rights under Articles 6
[3]
and 8
[4]
of the
Quebec
Charter of Human rights and Freedoms.
[5]

Zohar therefore merits a condemnation to punitive damages by virtue of
Article
49
of the
Charter
.  The Court believes that an award of
$30,000
to
Imaflex payable by Zohar alone will pay sufficient deference to the social
purposes of retribution and prevention that punitive damages are intended to
serve without being inconsistent with the jurisprudence on the subject.

104
.     The Court does not believe it necessary
or fair to impose punitive damages on the individual Defendants as well.
However excessive their reactions were, they may well have believed that
Imaflex did not intend to move until the end of the term and that, already in
arrears, it would make good its threat not to pay its outstanding bills.  Their
actions were not therefore totally devoid of any colour of right.  In the
circumstances, the Court believes that imposing the added burden of punitive
damages on them would be unduly harsh.  Holding them solidarily liable with
Zohar for $64,332 of compensatory damages is punishment enough.

SECTION 15 - EXCESS SCRAP

Disposition of the claim

105
.     This was a very ambitious claim for Imaflex to
make, and for all the reasons advanced by Zohar's counsel, most notably
contained in the report and the testimony of Zohar's expert  Ken Ahmedkhan, it
fails.

106
.     Mr. Ahmedkhan's technical credentials and
objectivity are impeccable.  A chemical engineer, he has spent more than 25
years in the flexible plastics business, including two years as Vice President
and general manager of Union Carbide's flexible packaging division.  He now is
part owner of and runs a plastic film business with $10,000,000 annual sales, a
business very similar to that of Imaflex, of which he happens also to be a
shareholder.

107
.     The Court took under advisement the recognition of
Joe Abbandonato and Gerry Phelps as expert witnesses.  While they also have
long experience in the business, and Mr. Phelps's technical qualifications are
impressive, neither is without personal interest in the outcome of the case.
Therefore, while the Court recognizes them as experts, it does not place the
same weight on their testimony as on that of Mr. Ahmedkhan whose qualifications
are at least as impressive, and whose neutrality the Court does not doubt.

108
.     The Court believes that the following
considerations in particular justify the rejection of Imaflex's claim for
excessive scrap:

109
.     There is really no such thing as an industry-wide
standard, at least none that Imaflex could prove.  What the Court retains is
that the standard will vary depending on other factors, particularly the nature
of the product being produced (garbage bag sheeting allowing room for more
tolerance than high-end products) and the size and frequency of orders.

110
.     Imaflex was not able to prove its pretension that
it was the incompetence and lack of availability of Zohar's employees assigned
to run the Dolci line that was the primary cause of excessive scrap levels.
Imaflex could not reliably establish the number of times this was the principal
factor or even a contributing factor.  Gerry Phelps's analysis appeared
speculative and based on assumptions as to acceptable scrap levels that were
unproven.

111
.     A more likely factor was the fact that until
Imaflex arrived, the Dolci line and most other machinery at Zohar had been used
to produce black garbage bags, the product demanding the least sophisticated
machinery, the lowest level of skill of operators and the least strict
precision of blends.  (Black plastic hides imperfections and blemishes that
would not be acceptable in the better quality - and higher priced - plastic
Imaflex wanted to sell.)  Ken Ahmedkhan testified that in order to eliminate
many of the problems Imaflex experienced, an expensive upgrade of the line
would have been necessary.  That, more than deficient labour appeared to be the
source of its problems in the estimation of the Court.  The Court is also
mindful of the fact that there was a break-in and training period for the Dolci
operators, of whom more would be expected, under Gerry Phelps's supervision.
By July 1, 1992 Mr. Phelps apparently believed they were ready.  What then
would have accounted for their regression?

112
.     (Aware of this difficulty Imaflex seems to have
concentrated its complaint more on the availability of the workers than their
talent.  In either case it seems to the Court Imaflex's complaints are the
stuff of case by case analysis rather than hypothesis based on elusive
industry-wide norms.)

113
.     Mr. Ahmedkhan believed that, considering the size
and frequency of orders, an acceptable scrap level would have been 20%.  The
rate on the Dolci line was in fact roughly 18% by his calculation, and 17% by
Gerry Phelps's.

114
.     The absence of an automatic scrap recovery system,
which the Agreement contemplated that Imaflex would add to the Dolci line,
significantly increased the scrap level, as Joe Abbandonato himself recognized
in May 1993 (Exhibit D-17).

115
.     In the absence of a contractual standard, the
obligation of Zohar is one of means, not result.

116
.     Finally, there is no way that the Court can
determine how much of the scrap that figures in Gerry Phelps's analysis was
either not recycled or not recyclable.  The only columns that appear designate
quantities of scrap and rejects.  Only scrap that cannot be recycled should
give rise to a claim for lost materials, assuming Imaflex's claim to be
otherwise well-founded.

117
.     In sum, Imaflex has failed to establish its claim
for excessive scrap through presumptions that are serious, precise and
concordant.

SECTION 16 - DOWN TIME DUE TO POOR MAINTENANCE
AND REPAIRS

Disposition of claim

118
.     Imaflex's claim fails, essentially for the same
general reasons as expressed in the Court's rejection of its claim for excess
scrap.  It could not prove an industry wide standard of acceptable down time.
Each situation varies, depending especially on the age of the machine.

119
.     In Exhibit P-51 Gerry Phelps calculated a total of
1057 hours of down time between October 1992 and August 1993, an 11 month
period.  In Schedule J of its Summary of Final Claims Imaflex notes a total of
1,247 hours of downtime for the same period.  It eliminates what it calls
routine maintenance and ends up claiming 164 hours for Jewish Sabbath closures
and 566 hours for what it calls excess maintenance downtime, or 730 hours in
all.

120
.     In the detailed analysis of the down time a
variety of maintenance related causes appear.  However, it is not possible to
establish that on a balance of probabilities the interruptions were mainly due
to inadequate maintenance or unacceptably slow reaction time.  All that the
Court is given is a claim in bulk for lost time with a general claim that it is
all Zohar's fault.

121
.     As for the Sabbaths and presumably other holy days
identified in the detailed summary as Jewish holidays during which the Premises
were closed, Imaflex presumably was aware of the fact that Zohar's principals
are observant Jews who do not work nor have their employees work on those
days.  Imaflex did not object until after the Agreement  was terminated.

122
.     Zohar gave no warranty that the Dolci line would
function without breakdown or interruption, only that it would maintain and
repair it.  Imaflex has not shown that Zohar defaulted in this respect.  All it
shows is that it was displeased with Zohar's level of performance.

123
.     In the absence of a contractually defined
standard, reasonable diligence in the performance of maintenance is all that
Imaflex had a right to expect.  It has failed to prove Zohar's failure to meet
that standard.

trial that it did not intend o advance any proof in support of its

TAB D: PERSONAL LIABILITY OF ZOHAR'S PRINCIPALS

Disposition of claim

128
.     There is no basis in law or fact to
hold the individual Defendants liable for any claim advanced by Imaflex, with
the exception of the damages arising from the September 1993 shutdown.  These
are justified by reason of the denial of access to the Premises, the retention
of finished goods and the removal of resin without permission.  The other
claims relate purely to operations in the normal course and even where
well-founded do not, as do the shutdown and related events, exhibit the element
of abuse that would justify lifting the corporate veil.  The solidary
condemnation of the individual Defendants is therefore limited to
$64,322

and the costs to that extent.

COSTS

129
.     Most of the burden of this litigation
was due to the fact that Imaflex's principals chose to make the case an
occasion to vent their enduring anger that arose from Imaflex's unhappy
commercial co-habitation with Zohar, notwithstanding that it has since
prospered as a public company.

130
.     The Court perceives that this
phenomenon greatly contributed to an inappropriate expansion of the claims to
unsustainable levels.  Much trial time, and undoubtedly enormous preparation
time as well, was devoted to the questions of excess scrap, down time and
missing inventory.  These resulted in a quagmire of suppositions and
calculations.

131
.     If there had been a genuine will to
settle, the missing inventory issue might have been resolved fairly readily.
As for the claims for excess scrap and down time, they were futile to begin
with.  Imaflex's level of dissatisfaction with Zohar's performance of the
Agreement was most appropriately dealt with by ending it.

132
.     It is perplexing that having announced
an intention to do so in December 1992, Imaflex should have lingered as long as
it did, all the while impugning Zohar's competence and good faith and
threatening to withhold payments.  While the latter's precipitous actions in
September 1993 can never be excused, they can perhaps be better understood in
these circumstances.

133
.     Furthermore, because the totality of
Imaflex's original claims in the staggering amount of $712,150 was directed
against the personal Defendants solidarily, they undoubtedly felt it necessary
to attempt to mount a countervailing attack in the form of a cross-demand that
may have been equally excessive.

134
.     Zohar at least had the good sense not
to pursue its cross-demand at trial.  Imaflex also had second thoughts about
some of its claims and reduced its total claim to $486,735, but persisted
nonetheless in seeking a solidary condemnation against the individual
Defendants, even though most of its claims were on their face devoid of the elements
of fraud or abuse that would justify piercing the corporate veil.

135
.     Purely technical Issues of down time,
excess scrap, and even missing inventory (considering the inherent risk of
confusion and Imaflex's passivity in that connection) would not normally incite
a desire to pursue officers of a corporation personally, unless of course the
pursuer had a particular axe to grind, which was manifestly the case here.

136
.     For these reasons, the costs will be
limited to those taxable on the net amount of the condemnation in the principal
demand, including experts' fees, with the exception, however, of the Christian
Dorais report on missing inventory and any fees of Gerry Phelps, and with the
individual Defendants' share of the costs being limited to their solidary
liability to pay them to the extent only of an action for $64,332.

SECTION 1 -
DOWN TIME DUE TO LATE START-UP

Imaflex's argument

The Agreement was entered into on December
9, 1991.  Between then and the time Zohar finally decided on a location for the
Oerlikon, February 10, 1992, which was the date the electricians were called to
commence work (Gerry Phelps’s testimony in chief, Exhibit P-4, Invoice No.
442459 from Ultratech) two months elapsed.

During that time Zohar was installing
another extruder for its own use (Serge Afflalo's testimony in
cross-examination, Gerry Phelps’s testimony in re-direct, Exhibit D-51 pp. 1,
2, 16, 20, 23, 25, 26, 27, 28, 29, 30, 31,32, detailing costs of installation
of the extruder).  Zohar was unwilling to  be inconvenienced by  Imaflex’s
needs and have the Oerlikon extruder installed in a timely manner.  It
concentrated its efforts on ensuring its own extruder was installed and
operating as quickly as possible and therefore could not give the same
attention to Imaflex’s installation of the Oerlikon.

Zohar had the obligation to
deliver the Dolci line to Imaflex in a reasonable time.  That time can be
determined by common usage of the industry. As testified by different
witnesses, (Joe Abbandonato’s testimony in chief, Gerry Phelps’s testimony in
chief, Robert Krycki expert witness in chief, Dr. Basilio Yi expert witness in
chief) the reasonable time to install both lines was 6 to 8 weeks.

Therefore, Zohar was in default
to deliver the Dolci line at any time past the 8 week limit since the
obligation of delivery is essential to a lease agreement.

Serge Afflalo testified that it would have
been illogical for Zohar to deliver the Dolci line to Imaflex at the same time
that Imaflex delivered the Oerlikon line to Zohar since Zohar was already
operating and had production requirements to be met.  (Serge Afflalo testimony
in cross-examination).

This argument is unfounded.  Firstly,
Zohar had other extrusion lines operating and could have easily transferred
production from the Dolci to the other extruders.  Secondly, it could have
transferred the production from the Dolci to the new extruder Zohar had just
installed as it takes a few months to book a new extrusion line (Joe
Abbandonato’s testimony in chief).

If it was illogical for Zohar to stop
production on its Dolci, then the same reasoning must apply to Imaflex, that
is, it was illogical for Imaflex to wait until the Oerlikon was installed in
order to start adapting the Dolci for its needs.

Full-scale production was begun
by Imaflex only on July 1, 1992 (Exhibit P-5), over 90 days after it should
have started production.  Imaflex is therefore claiming 90 days of down time as
a result of the late start-up due entirely to Zohar’s actions.

Joe Abbandonato testified that he
complained to Jules Amar on several occasions about the delay in the start up
of production.  (Joe Abbandonato’s testimony in chief).  Gerry Phelps also
testified that he asked Serge Afflalo on several occasions about the final
location and the start up.  (Gerry Phelps’s testimony in chief).

Written notice of default not
necessary

Imaflex argues Imaflex put
Zohar in default of its obligation to deliver the Dolci line in a timely
manner, even if not in writing.  Baudoin states that a written default is not
necessarily peremptory for article 1067 C.C.L.C. to be applicable:

(…) ”alors que certains arrêts, au contraire, considèrent
l’exigence de la forme écrite comme une simple règle de preuve, Cette dernière
opinion nous paraît  préférable, En effet, la mise en demeure étant une simple
indication de la volonté du créancier, il semble illogique que la loi ait voulu
en faire un acte à caractère solennel. Ce qui importe, c’est qu’elle soit
sérieuse et puisse être prouvée.
[6]
»

The Court of Quebec
[7]
as well as the Quebec Court of Appeal
[8]
have both held that a verbal default
notice is sufficient.

Furthermore, this delay in the
start up took place at the inception of the parties’ relationship, at a time
when Imaflex believed in the good faith of Zohar and did not want to sour their
relationship and believed that a written notice was not necessary (Joe
Abbandonato’s testimony in chief.)  At no time did Imaflex ever renounce to
its rights to this claim. It is a reasonable expectation of Imaflex to have
expected Zohar’s good faith since it is a general duty imposed in contractual
relationships ( Art. 1024 C.C.L.C.)
[9]

Based on established case law, Imaflex
argues it has a right, to claim for foregone normal profits.

The $700 a day lost
contribution claimed by Imaflex is detailed under the heading “SHUTDOWN AFTER
SEPTEMBER 2, 1993” in Section 8.

Therefore the amount
claimed by Imaflex is $63,000:             (90 days X $700/day = $63,000).

Zohar's response

There existed no contractual obligation
incumbent upon Defendants, the Agreement being silent as to the chronology of
the transfer of the two lines.

Furthermore, all evidence shows that the
parties never even discussed the issue prior to its signature.  Serge Afflalo's
testimony is clearly to the effect that he understood and assumed that the
Dolci line would only be transferred to Imaflex for modification once the
Oerlikon had been properly transferred to Zohar for its production.  He
considered this to be the rational and logical approach because Zohar was not
prepared to reduce its productivity for any period of time pending
implementation of the contract.  Contrary to Imaflex's arguments, there is no
evidence to suggest that Zohar could have easily replaced the Dolci's
productivity with its existing extruders.

On the contrary, the evidence suggests,
and it is merely common sense to assume that it was reasonable for Zohar to
conclude that if it had interrupted operation on the Dolci line during the
period when the Oerlikon was being installed, its productivity would have been
affected.

Since the Agreement was drafted and
prepared by Imaflex's representatives, its silence on this issue and any
resulting misunderstanding between the parties, must be resolved in favour of
Defendant and the Agreement interpreted against Imaflex.  Thus, in insisting
that the Oerlikon line be properly and functionally transferred to Zohar prior
to the latter transferring the Dolci line to Imaflex, Zohar violated no
contractual obligation.

In any event, the subsequent conduct of
the parties during the relevant period corroborates Zohar's interpretation.
While the testimony offered by Imaflex indicates there may have been some
grumbling by Joe Abbandonato and Gerry Phelps, the first time Imaflex advised
Zohar it considered the "late start-up" to be a breach of contract
was almost two years later when the present proceedings were instituted.  In
effect, during the relevant period, that is between January and April of 1992,
Imaflex clearly acquiesced to Zohar's interpretation of the Agreement by
failing put it in default.

Such inaction bars Imaflex's entitlement
to claim damages in relation to the alleged breach of contract referred to
hereinabove.

SECTION 2 -
QUALITY CLAIMS

Imaflex's
argument

Paragraph 10 of the Agreement
states:

that if it is determined that the product is not acceptable
to Imaflex’s customer because formulas were not followed or proper machine
settings were not made or quality control checks were not followed then the raw
materials used in that production run will be charged to Zohar and the fee for
that run will not be paid to Zohar.  It is understood that this clause only
comes into effect once all parties agree that Zohar’s employees have acquired
the technical expertise from G. Phelps.

Imaflex’s only obligation is
therefore to prove that the product was not acceptable to the customer.
Imaflex suffered several quality related problems with its customers (Joe
Abbandonato’s testimony in chief) and claims the following damages:

Packaging Group Claim (Exhibit
P-71)

Francis Chantiam, C.E.O. of the
Packaging Group, testified that on several occasions, products delivered by
Imaflex were of poor quality, as evidenced by  Exhibit P-71 relating to a
customer complaint report concerning a low  treatment level and poor adhesive
bond strength; which are all directly  attributable to Zohar’s fault.

extruder and the person they were paying to maintain and repair it, Zohar, did
not carry enough spare parts to mitigate downtime.

Zohar knew or should have known which
parts were essential to carry in inventory and knowing the Dolci was Imaflex’s
only extruder, it had a higher degree of care for its maintenance.

Serge Afflalo's testimony on this matter
again contradicted the Imaflex's claim.  He states that all consumable items
were in stock, including TCW.  However, Imaflex's claim indicated that the
Dolci line did not have the proper TCW in stock.  (Serge Afflalo's testimony in
chief)  He states further that having control boards in stock would be like
having another machine in stock.  Gerry Phelps’s testimony that one board is
interchangeable with any one of the five boards on the Dolci is corroborated by
Ken’s testimony.  Serge Afflalo admits that a control board costs anywhere from
a few hundred dollars to $1,000. (Serge Afflalo's testimony in
cross-examination)  Would it not have been prudent for Zohar to carry at least
one spare board in the event that any one of the five boards failed?  Would it
not have been the minimum expected under the circumstances?

On some occasions, while Imaflex was
experiencing down time on the Dolci, Zohar was benefiting from operating the
Dolci for its own use while continuing to use the Oerlikon.  On one occasion,
Gerry Phelps had to order Zohar’s production off the Dolci after repeated
requests (Gerry Phelps’s testimony  in re-direct, Joe Abbandonato’s testimony
in chief).

Because Zohar failed to meet its
contractual obligations with respect to maintenance and repairs of the Dolci
extruder, Imaflex suffered excessive down time due to poor maintenance which is
hereby claimed in the amount of $24,407.92 (Summary of Final Claims - Schedule
J).

Zohar's response

Imaflex claims $24,407.92 for
excessive down time it allegedly suffered as a result of Zohar's poor maintenance
of the machinery and this is the case even though Imaflex has provided
virtually no evidence to prove that most of the down time was actually
attributable to specific events which were Zohar's fault.

In fact, apart from broad
generalizations of Messrs. Phelps and Joe Abbandonato and the statistical
analysis of down time prepared by Mr. Phelps, which is clearly insufficient in
order to meet a burden of proof of fault, Imaflex offered evidence for only two
specific cases of mechanical problems.

The evidence tendered with
respect to the two cases failed to establish negligence.

A)         At one point during
his testimony Gerry Phelps spoke of a breakdown  of the Dolci which he actually
attributed to improper greasing.  According to him Zohar did not use top grade
grease which was necessary for a machine such as the Dolci.  As a result, he
claimed that the Dolci suffered mechanical failure that led to several hundred
hours of downtime.  That is the extent of the evidence with respect to that
incident.

Serge Afflalo testified that
the Dolci was regularly greased and that the grease used was in fact top grade
and adequate for the Dolci, having been recommended by a company experienced in
the operation of such machinery.

He further testified that the
mechanical failure to which Gerry Phelps was referring was in fact caused by a
control board short circuit and was in fact replaced as quickly as possible.

Imaflex has failed to meet the
burden of proof that, on the balance of probabilities, Zohar was at fault with
respect to that specific incident.

B)         Gerry Phelps also
referred to the problem with the oscillating thermocouple cable.  According to
him most of the down time incurred because of the problem with the oscillating
thermocouple cable was due to Zohar's faulty maintenance practices.

However, no evidence other than
his testimony was offered to prove the allegations.

In defence, Serge Afflalo
testified that when the thermocouple cable first snapped, he and Zohar's
mechanic discussed replacing the cable with Phelps who concurred in the choice
of the replacement cable.  This testimony was in fact corroborated by Mr.
Phelps in cross examination.

In fact, he also testified that
at the time he figured that the replacement cable required was a standard
industry cable and not a specialized type.

Thus Mr. Phelps, "a
professional engineer with extensive experience in the extrusion industry"
(as he is described in Imaflex's notes and authorities), agreed with the
diagnosis of Serge Afflalo and the mechanic.  In fact, it was he who referred
Afflalo to the supplier of the first replacement cable.

When the problem persisted,
Afflalo testified, and Phelps confirmed in cross examination, that Phelps
continued to consult with Afflalo and the to find the solution to the problem.
The solution was not immediately obvious to either of the parties.

The solution to the problem was
only determined when Afflalo's representatives communicated with a company
known as Salerno which had operated one or more of the Dolci lines for several years.

As a result of the consultation
with Salerno, it was determined by all parties involved that a special type of
cable was required that could only be obtained from the manufacturer in Italy.

According to the testimony of
Afflalo and Phelps, Jules Amar, who was then in Italy, communicated with Dolci
in order to obtain the wire.  According to Afflalo's testimony, Dolci Italy did
not then have the cable in stock.

Once the cable was received,
Afflalo's testified, Zohar's representatives promptly installed it on the
machine.

On the basis of the above facts
proven at trial, it is difficult to understand how Phelps could possibly
reproach Zohar for the down time.

Phelps himself, Imaflex's
technical expert, failed to realise the necessity of installing specialised
cabling.

He participated with Zohar in
numerous and unsuccessful attempts to find a solution to the problem.  Zohar's
representatives acted in a reasonable and diligent manner.  Thus, Imaflex did
not meet its burden of proof establishing Zohar's fault with respect to the
down time resulting from the problem with the oscillating thermocouple cable.

Apart from the two incidents
described above, there are no specific and particularized allegations nor proof
of fault on the part of Defendant.  Imaflex attempts to impute Defendant's
fault for the balance of the down time, asking the Court to draw a presumption
from the fact that such down time was supposedly excessive according to
constantly moving and unproven industry standards.

The application of such standards
to judge Zohar's conduct is unfounded in law and in equity.  Imaflex's use of
such standards and the supposed statistical analyses put Defendant in an
intolerable position since it is not faced with any specific facts or incidents
to which it can respond in an intelligent and factual manner, as Defendant has
done with respect to the "grease" and "thermocouple"
incidents.

Furthermore, without prejudice
to the foregoing, Zohar demonstrated that it had implemented a general and
reasonable maintenance policy and that the machinery was regularly checked and
maintained, that a reasonable inventory of spare parts were kept on the
Premises and that Zohar employed two mechanics in order to carry out its
maintenance policy.

Imaflex's reply

Imaflex chooses to ignore
Exhibits P-51, P-51A and P-122 which state in great detail and based on
specific dates, events, and hours the down time resulting from poor maintenance
and repair.

Zohar does not contest its
contractual obligation to maintain the equipment, which constitutes an
obligation of result.

Zohar's counsel simply
discusses two incidents: one related to improper grease and the second dealing
with thermocouple wiring (TCW)

On the issue of the grease the
Court is confronted with two opposing versions of the same incident, one
related by Gerry Phelps, an experienced engineer in the plastics industry and
another by Serge Afflalo, who has a background in agriculture and basically
learned “on the job”.  Phelps ’s version is credible while Afflalo's is not.
We are asked to believe Serge who makes general statements that the Dolci was
greased.  How often?  With what grease?  By whom?

Serge Afflalo admitted that
Zohar did not keep a maintenance log but repaired and maintained equipment and
machinery only when necessary.  Gerry Phelps testified that the grease he
recommended was not used by Zohar because it was costlier.  This is consistent
with Zohar’s behaviour throughout the relevant period as well as the testimony
of the personal Defendants.  The Defendants were penny wise and pound foolish.

Zohar places great emphasis on
the fact that Gerry Phelps was consulted by Serge Afflalo to discuss the TCW
issue.  However, the contractual obligation to maintain and repair the
equipment was that of Zohar and Gerry Phelps was not a consultant at the time.
If he was, then Zohar had an obligation to pay his consulting fees.  If he was
not, then Zohar cannot find fault with his actions.  Zohar cannot have it both
ways.

Moreover, Zohar again fails to
address the issue of the circuit boards.  Several hours of downtime were caused
by Zohar’s failure to stock circuit boards.  Zohar’s own expert witness, Ken
Ahmedkhan agreed that if he had only one extruder he would keep more than one
circuit board in stock, knowing full well that if a circuit board failed, he
would easily replace it and minimally disrupt production.

Zohar knew Imaflex only had the
one production line and in those circumstances knew or should have known that
it was prudent to stock at least one circuit board.  Its failure to do so
resulted in a complete shutdown of Imaflex’s production for several days.

Furthermore, Robert Krycki’s
expert testimony is not contradicted whereby he states that down time should be
between 200 -- 240 hour per year.  Imaflex experienced considerably greater
down time directly resulting from Zohar’s
maintenance policy as detailed in Plaintiff’s Written Pleadings.
